extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy; readers of Locke's Essay concerning Human Understanding
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting Locke's conceptual criteria about how the mind acquires ideas and the distinctions among modes of ideas, thinking, passions, power, liberty, and related concepts as presented in the selected chapters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin of ideas: sensation and reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: All our simple ideas come to the mind only by sensation and reflection; even ideas that seem remote from sense (e.g., infinity) are ultimately derived from these sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke repeatedly asserts that the first ideas we have are received by the senses and by reflection on our own mental operations. He allows that specialized mathematicians may introduce other ways later, but maintains the first and primary origin is sensation and reflection. Examples include the ideas of duration, space, and number.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas of infinity are not positive/comprehensive ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: We do not possess clear, positive, comprehensive ideas of infinity; if we did, we could sensibly add infinities together, which leads to absurdities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke argues that if anyone claimed a positive idea of infinite duration or space, they would be able to add two infinites and make one infinitely bigger than another — an absurdity showing our idea of infinity is negative/derived, not a directly grasped positive magnitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idea of infinite space/duration independent of existing matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Having the idea of infinite space does not imply the real existence of infinite matter; the mind can conceive empty space or duration without corresponding existing bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke gives analogies (a bushel without corn; a nut-shell without a kernel) and contrasts infinite duration (often thought of because of God's eternity) with infinite space to show that conception does not require real instantiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex/extended ideas formed by repetition and composition of simple ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: The mind forms modes and complex ideas by repeating, compounding, and putting together simple ideas received from sensation and reflection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modes such as extended durations, sizeable spaces, tunes, or complex tastes arise from the mind's ability to repeat and combine simple sensory impressions; mathematical or advanced speculations may refine this but the basic mechanism is repetition/composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of motion as distinct simple modes
rubrics_metrics.description: Different modifications of motion (slide, roll, tumble, walk, creep, run, dance, leap, skip, etc.) are distinct simple modes of the idea of motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motion-modes correspond to measures combining time and space; they are complex ideas encompassing both extension and duration. Locke lists many motion-words as examples that immediately call distinct ideas to mind for English speakers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of sounds and silent formation of tunes
rubrics_metrics.description: Varieties of sounds and their arrangements (e.g., a tune) are modes of the sense of hearing; a musician can form the idea of a tune by reflecting on component notes even when no sound is present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke uses 'tune' to show that complex auditory ideas can be constructed in the mind from simpler sound-ideas and that such formation can occur without external stimulation (imagination/mental rehearsal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of colour often constitute mixed modes with figure
rubrics_metrics.description: Many notable colour-modes are mixed modes because colour-assemblages commonly involve figure as well (as in painting, weaving), producing complex ideas like beauty or rainbow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because assemblages of colours in art involve figure plus colour, these complex ideas are classified as mixed modes rather than pure simple modes of colour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compound tastes and smells are modes often unnamed
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounded tastes and smells form modes that are numerous but typically lack distinct names and are less frequently recorded in writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke notes that these sensory modes are meaningful in experience but often omitted from explicit categorization due to lack of general utility or difficulty of semanticizing them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Many simple modes have no names due to limited usefulness or fine gradation
rubrics_metrics.description: Many distinct simple modes (often slight degrees of the same quality) have no distinct names, either because measures to distinguish them are lacking or because they are not useful enough to have been named by common speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke suggests naming is driven by human concerns for communication and usefulness: actions and items central to daily life get precise named complex ideas, while fine perceptual gradations do not. Examples of named technical complex ideas: 'cohobation', 'filtration', 'drilling' (terms in crafts and chemistry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming is governed by frequency of use and communicative purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Words and distinct names are given to complex ideas primarily where rapid, efficient communication about frequent or important human activities is needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke explains that arts and trades develop terms for their habitual complex ideas to facilitate quick direction and discourse; those outside a craft commonly do not understand these names because they lack the habitual formation of those complex ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of thinking: catalogue of inner modifications
rubrics_metrics.description: When the mind contemplates its own actions it discerns many modes: SENSATION, REMEMBRANCE, RECOLLECTION, CONTEMPLATION, REVERIE, ATTENTION, INTENTION/STUDY, DREAMING, ECSTASY, etc., each delivering a distinct idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke defines each briefly: 'sensation' as perception accompanying an external impression; 'remembrance' when that idea recurs without the external object; 'recollection' when sought with effort; 'contemplation' when held under attentive consideration; 'reverie' as ideas floating without reflection; 'attention' as registering ideas in memory; 'intention/study' as fixing the mind earnestly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degrees of attention as meaningful distinctions in thinking
rubrics_metrics.description: The mind experiences varied degrees of attention — from intense focused study to near absence of thought — and this gradation is important to understanding mental operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke uses examples (fixing on an object to the exclusion of senses; barely observing trains of ideas; nearly no attention) to demonstrate that attention is a variable operation, not a binary state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thinking is likely an action (operation) not the essence of the soul
rubrics_metrics.description: Because thinking admits degrees, can be present or absent (sleep, dreaming), Locke argues it is probable that thinking is an action performed by the soul rather than the unvarying essence of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This philosophical conclusion follows from phenomenology: mental operations vary and can cease (sleep), which supports the view that thinking is an operant activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure and pain are simple ideas known only by experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure and pain are fundamental simple ideas acquired via sensation and reflection; they cannot be defined except by invoking the experience of their presence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke warns against defining pleasure/pain abstractly as 'good' or 'evil' without reference to the felt experience; the way to know these ideas is by attending to one's own feelings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good and evil are relative to pleasure and pain
rubrics_metrics.description: Things are called GOOD if apt to cause or increase pleasure or diminish pain (or procure other goods); conversely EVIL if apt to produce or increase pain or diminish pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke frames moral-valence language in hedonic terms. He includes bodily and mental pleasures/pains under these definitions and notes that they operate to move the passions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passions are caused by perceptions of good and evil (pleasure/pain)
rubrics_metrics.description: Our passions (love, hatred, desire, joy, sorrow, hope, fear, despair, anger, envy, etc.) arise from our perceptions of things as causes of pleasure or pain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke explains each passion as a disposition relative to pleasure/pain: love = thought of delight from something; hatred = thought of pain from something; desire = uneasiness from absence of an enjoyed good; joy, sorrow, hope, fear, despair, anger, envy are similarly tied to anticipations or experiences of pleasure/pain and relations to others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of key passions (compact list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Locke gives succinct definitions: LOVE (delight at present/absent thing), HATRED (thought of pain apt to be produced), DESIRE (uneasiness at absence of a desired good), JOY (delight from present or assured approaching possession), SORROW (uneasiness at loss or present evil), HOPE (pleasure in thought of probable future enjoyment), FEAR (uneasiness at thought of probable future evil), DESPAIR (thought of unattainableness of good), ANGER (uneasiness on receipt of injury with purpose of revenge), ENVY (uneasiness on seeing another obtain a desired good), SHAME (uneasiness on thought of indecent act or loss of esteem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke notes the list is not exhaustive and that each passion could be treated at greater length; some passions (envy, anger) involve considerations of self and others and so are not found in all humans, while many others (love, desire, hope, fear) are universal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal or lessening of pain counts as pleasure and vice versa
rubrics_metrics.description: In terms of passions, the removal or diminution of a pain is considered and operates as a pleasure; the loss or diminution of a pleasure is considered a pain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This observation affects how passions respond to changes in our circumstances and explains certain emotional reactions (relief as pleasure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Passions may have bodily effects but those are not essential to their idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Many passions produce bodily changes (e.g., shame sometimes causes blushing), but such physical operations are not essential parts of the definition of the passion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke cautions not to conflate bodily signs with the mental idea of a passion; some persons may experience the passion without the bodily concomitant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idea of power arises from observing regular changes and reflecting on operations
rubrics_metrics.description: The mind forms the idea of POWER by noting that one thing changes another and reflecting on observed regularities and possibilities of making or receiving change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: fire's power to melt gold; sun's power to whiten wax. Power is considered relative to observable changes in sensible ideas; the mind abstracts a power capable of producing or receiving such changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active and passive power distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Power is twofold: ACTIVE (ability to make change) and PASSIVE (ability to receive change).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke points out that bodies seem to show passive power (receiving change) and transfer motion, but the clearest idea of active power (the ability to begin actions) is observed in thinking agents (spirits) by reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power includes relational components
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea of power includes relation (to action or change) because almost all ideas when considered involve relations among parts, causes, or effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke observes that extension, duration, number, figure, motion, and sensible qualities all involve relations; 'power' is similar in containing relational content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearest idea of active power comes from reflection on mental action (spirit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bodies provide an obscure idea of active power (they appear to transfer rather than originate motion); reflection on willing and the mind's ability to initiate motion or thought gives the clearest idea of active power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke uses the example of willing to move body parts as evidence that we know initiating power from introspection; physical interactions (impulse) only show transmission/continuation, not origination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Will and understanding as named powers (faculties) but not distinct substances
rubrics_metrics.description: Will (power to begin/forbear actions) and understanding (perceptive power) are commonly called 'faculties', yet Locke warns against treating these words as names for real distinct beings within the soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He suggests using such terms carefully to avoid metaphysical confusion; they denote capacities or powers observed in the mind, not necessarily separate entities doing the acting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas of liberty and necessity derive from extent of mental control
rubrics_metrics.description: From one's experience of the mind's power to begin/forbear actions arises the idea of LIBERTY (power to do or forbear according to the mind) and its opposite NECESSITY (where such power is absent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke defines liberty precisely: an agent is free insofar as doing or not doing a particular action is in the agent's power to be produced by volition. Examples: a tennis-ball is not a free agent; a locked person may act voluntarily (prefer to stay) but not freely (cannot forbear staying).

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty is distinct from volition/being voluntary
rubrics_metrics.description: Volition (preference or willing) does not guarantee liberty; an action can be voluntary yet not free if the power to do otherwise is absent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke contrasts cases (convulsive motions, being locked in a room) to show that voluntary preferring differs from the metaphysical condition of liberty, which requires the power to produce or forbear the action according to the mind's choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary opposed to involuntary
rubrics_metrics.description: Locke begins to distinguish voluntary actions (those accompanied by thought or volition) from involuntary actions, implying a criterion based on presence/absence of mental direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the chapter cuts off here, the guiding idea is that voluntary actions are performed under the direction of the mind (will/volition), whereas involuntary actions occur without such mental command; previous examples (sleep-transported person who stays willingly but not freely) illustrate the distinction.
